claims.text: Increasing configurational entropy in a spinel oxide support enhances catalytic activity under dry, lean CO-oxidation conditions.
Increasing configurational entropy in a spinel oxide improves resistance to catalytic deactivation.
A high-entropy spinel support can enable lower platinum-group-metal consumption without sacrificing performance.
The relevant conventional automotive baseline is a 4-metal spinel catalyst with standard platinum-group-metal loading.
A 7-metal spinel has greater configurational disorder than the 4-metal spinel comparator.
A high-entropy spinel support will disperse and isolate platinum-group metals as highly dispersed or single-atom sites.
The proposed improvement applies over approximately 150–500 °C under dry, oxygen-rich automotive exhaust conditions.
The multi-element spinel lattice has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
High configurational entropy enhances oxygen-vacancy formation in the spinel.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation in the spinel.
The uniform distribution of multiple cations enhances electronic conductivity.
The high-entropy spinel stabilizes isolated platinum-group-metal sites against sintering and deactivation.
The proposed structural and electronic changes lower the activation barrier for CO oxidation.
A 7-metal high-entropy spinel achieves a T10 of 168 °C compared with 454 °C for a 4-metal spinel, corresponding to about a 63% decrease.
A platinum-group-metal-bearing 7-metal high-entropy catalyst will show an approximately 60% lower light-off temperature than a conventionally loaded automotive 4-metal spinel catalyst.
The 7-metal high-entropy spinel has better long-term stability than the 4-metal spinel, with 4.7% rather than 12.2% activity loss over 14 hours.
The durability advantage will persist for a reduced-PGM catalyst under automotive operational conditions.
The benefit may be less pronounced in moist, sulfur-containing, or rich exhaust.
